Daily Transit Intelligence
June 23, 2026 — 12 papers analyzed
KEY FINDINGS
A Car Dependency Index across 18 cities shows car dependency persists even
after controlling for income, and isolated metro lines yield only local gains.
GPS-based mobility data in Mexico shows source-specific, spatially clustered
coverage bias — Facebook and multi-app data paint different portraits.
Transit's link to social mixing holds in large metros but fades to
insignificance in smaller Swedish cities once geography is controlled for.
PAPER OF THE DAY
Car Dependency in Urban Accessibility
Bruno Campanelli, Francesco Marzolla, Matteo Bruno, Hygor Piaget Monteiro Melo, Vittorio Loreto
A new Car Dependency Index measured across 18 cities in Europe and North America finds that car
dependency persists even after controlling for income. A "what-if" simulation of Rome's planned
Metro C expansion predicts roughly 60,000 fewer commuting vehicles — but the effect is localized,
reinforcing that systemic, network-level transit expansion is needed to truly dismantle car reliance.

ACTIONABLE TAKEAWAYS
Cities pursuing single flagship rail extensions should pair them with network-level multimodal
investment; the Rome simulation suggests isolated lines underdeliver on systemic car-
dependency reduction.
Researchers using commercial GPS mobility data in data-scarce regions should explicitly test
for vendor-specific coverage bias rather than treating any single source as ground truth.
Agencies piloting fare-free bus programs can cite the NYC simulation's finding that fare-free
buses meaningfully help lower-income riders with only modest revenue trade-offs.
Mid-size cities should not assume transit investment automatically increases social mixing as
it appears to in large metros; targeted venue-level interventions may work better.
Smart-city dashboards pairing ridership with air-quality metrics should avoid implying a
universal causal relationship; baseline city effects dominate over any consistent pattern.
